Nilpotent Jacobian maps in dimension three
and stable tameness in block extensions

Jie Wang Address: Jie Wang, State Key Laboratory of Mathematical Sciences, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Email address: wangjie212@amss.ac.cn and Dan Yan Address: Dan Yan, MOE-LCSM, School of Mathematics and Statistics, Hunan Normal University, Changsha, China Email address: yan-dan-hi@163.com
Date: September 11, 2026
Abstract.

We study polynomial maps in three variables with nilpotent Jacobian over a field of characteristic zero. The proposed classification reduces maps with linearly independent components to a family determined by a univariate polynomial evaluated at a quadratic coordinate. The geometric part of the argument produces two algebraically dependent constant linear combinations of the components. A derivation argument then yields the normal form over the original field. We obtain explicit polynomial inverses and tame factorizations. We then study higher-dimensional maps in which all but the last three components depend on three variables. For this class, we give separate normal forms for the two three-variable blocks and deduce stable tameness from the residue-field criterion of Berson, van den Essen, and Wright.

Key words and phrases: 
Nilpotent Jacobian, polynomial automorphism, linear conjugation, generic fiber, tame automorphism, stable tameness
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14R15; Secondary 14R10, 13N15

1. Introduction

Let KK be a field of characteristic zero. Keller’s Jacobian conjecture asserts that a polynomial map F:Kn→KnF\colon K^{n}\to K^{n} with detJ​F∈K∗\det JF\in K^{*} has a polynomial inverse. Introduced by Keller [14], the problem connects the geometry of affine space with the structure of polynomial algebras. For background on polynomial automorphisms, see [18]; for a recent account of the topology of polynomial maps, their nonproperness loci, and connections with the Jacobian conjecture, see El Hilany [10].

The status of the general conjecture changed in July 2026 with Alpöge’s three-dimensional counterexample. Tao [17] gives a geometric exposition of the example, while Gao [11] develops the tangent-sweep construction and its higher-dimensional extensions. The original map has constant Jacobian determinant −2-2 and identifies three distinct points. These developments show that the general Keller condition does not imply global invertibility in dimension at least three. They also require a distinction between that condition and the more restrictive nilpotent-Jacobian hypotheses studied here.

The reductions of Bass, Connell, and Wright [2] and Yagzhev [19] reduce the general conjecture to maps F=id+HF=\id+H with HH cubic homogeneous and J​HJH nilpotent, with the dimension allowed to vary. These reductions can increase the dimension. Consequently, counterexamples to the general conjecture yield counterexamples within the reduced class in some dimension, but this argument does not determine the three-variable case with J​HJH nilpotent.

Recent work also examines the algebraic constraints imposed by the Jacobian condition. Lee and Li [15] use generalized Magnus expansions to obtain restrictions on the Newton polygons of inner polynomials associated with planar Jacobian pairs. Ramírez and Valqui [16] compute a Gröbner basis and describe the solution set of a polynomial system arising in a Laurent-series formulation of the planar problem. In a different direction, Hamada, Kato, and Komiya [12] relate a Tate-algebra version of the conjecture to the polynomial version under a Hausdorff adic-topology hypothesis. These approaches complement the study of normal forms, generic fibers, and explicit inverses pursued below.

Nilpotence also suggests a structural question. If H⁡(0)=0H(0)=0 and J​HJH is nilpotent, must the components of HH be linearly dependent over KK? The answer is affirmative in dimension two and, in any dimension, when the Jacobian has rank at most one; see [2, 8]. For homogeneous maps in dimension three, de Bondt and van den Essen proved the stronger conclusion of linear triangularizability [7]. The general dependence problem has counterexamples, including homogeneous counterexamples in higher dimensions [9]. Thus a classification in dimension three must account for maps with linearly independent components.

Several classifications treat the case of independent components under additional hypotheses. Chamberland and van den Essen [6] considered maps

H=(u⁡(x,y),v⁡(x,y,z),h⁡(u⁡(x,y),v⁡(x,y,z))).H=\bigl(u(x,y),v(x,y,z),h(u(x,y),v(x,y,z))\bigr).

Yan and Tang [21] studied restrictions on the degree in zz, and Yan and de Bondt [20] treated related forms in arbitrary dimension. Classifications under further restrictions on variable dependence appear in [5, 22]. The manuscript of He and Yan [13] studies maps (u⁡(x,y),v⁡(x,y,z),h⁡(x,y,z))(u(x,y),v(x,y,z),h(x,y,z)) under the inequality degz⁡v≥2​degz​h\deg_{z}v\geq 2\deg_{z}h, and also treats the case degz⁡h≤3\deg_{z}h\leq 3. Its Problem 4.1 asks whether a common normal form remains valid without these restrictions.

This paper develops a classification of normalized three-variable maps with independent components and nilpotent Jacobian, and studies its consequences for tame and stably tame automorphisms. The argument is based on the family

(1.1) 𝒩P​(x,y,z)=(P⁡(y+x2),z−2​x​P​(y+x2),P​(y+x2)2),P∈K⁡[t]∖K,P⁡(0)=0.\mathcal{N}_{P}(x,y,z)=\bigl(P(y+x^{2}),\ z-2xP(y+x^{2}),\ P(y+x^{2})^{2}\bigr),\qquad P\in K[t]\setminus K,\quad P(0)=0.

Its Jacobian is nilpotent, and its components are linearly independent. Moreover, if

(X,Y,Z)=(x,y,z)+s​𝒩P​(x,y,z),(X,Y,Z)=(x,y,z)+s\mathcal{N}_{P}(x,y,z),

then the identity

(1.2) Y+X2−s​Z=y+x2Y+X^{2}-sZ=y+x^{2}

immediately gives a polynomial inverse. The main task is to reduce an arbitrary normalized map with independent components to this family.

The argument has two parts. First, Theorem 3.1 gives independent constant linear forms ℓ1,ℓ2\ell_{1},\ell_{2} for which ℓ1​(H)\ell_{1}(H) and ℓ2​(H)\ell_{2}(H) are algebraically dependent. To find them, we pass from the image field to its relative algebraic closure in K⁡(x,y,z)K(x,y,z). Over this field, the generic curve is contained in an affine plane and satisfies an equation of degree at most two. Homogeneous triangularization restricts its directions at infinity. We exclude the line case and the conic with two distinct points at infinity; the remaining conic yields the dependent pair. A quadratic relation among the components then yields descent to KK.

Second, Proposition 4.2 converts a dependent pair into (1.1). After writing the pair as f⁡(r),g⁡(r)f(r),g(r), we use a rational derivation with a slice to control the third component. A unit calculation rules out nonlinear dependence on a second invariant. Two commuting affine locally nilpotent derivations then show that rr is a polynomial in a coordinate y+Q⁡(x,z)y+Q(x,z), where deg⁡Q≤2\deg Q\leq 2. The remaining nilpotence identity forces the quadratic part of QQ to have rank one. Constant linear changes of coordinates complete the normalization. These changes are defined over KK and do not require the extraction of roots.

The resulting classification is stated in Theorem 4.1. It leads to Theorem 4.6: for H∈K​[x,y,z]3H\in K[x,y,z]^{3} with nilpotent Jacobian, the map id+H\id+H is tame. In the independent case we give an elementary factorization valid for the whole family id+s​H\id+sH over K⁡[s]K[s]. In the dependent case, a constant linear conjugation makes one component vanish. A primitive relation over K⁡[z]K[z] then produces a polynomial change of basis in the remaining two coordinates. This gives a tame factorization over K⁡[s]K[s] as well.

We next consider maps in dimension n≥6n\geq 6 of the form

(1.3) H~=(H1​(x1,x2,x3),…,Hn−3​(x1,x2,x3),Hn−2​(x),Hn−1​(x),Hn​(x)).\widetilde{H}=\bigl(H_{1}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}),\ldots,H_{n-3}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}),H_{n-2}(x),H_{n-1}(x),H_{n}(x)\bigr).

Two three-variable nilpotent Jacobians occur as diagonal blocks of J​H~J\widetilde{H}. Theorem 5.1 gives their normal forms, using the fraction field of the base ring for the last block. This operation must be distinguished from conjugation of the full map by a matrix with variable coefficients. The constant term of the last block with respect to its three variables must also be subtracted.

The stable-tameness conclusion does not require descent of these rational changes of coordinates. We first show that the last block defines an automorphism over the polynomial base ring. Every residue-field specialization is tame by Theorem 4.6. The residue-field criterion of Berson, van den Essen, and Wright [3, Theorem 4.12] then gives stable tameness over that ring. Together with the tame base map and Suslin’s theorem on polynomial matrices, this proves Theorem 5.6 for (1.3).

Section 2 introduces the notation and records the algebraic results used below. Section 3 contains the dependent-pair argument. Section 4 gives the classification and tame factorizations. Section 5 treats the higher-dimensional extensions. We conclude in Section 6 with several further questions.

2. Notation and preliminaries

Throughout the paper, KK denotes a field of characteristic zero. Polynomial maps and tuples of variables are written as column vectors. For H∈K​[x1,…,xn]nH\in K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]^{n}, we write

J​H=(∂Hi∂xj)1≤i,j≤n.JH=\left(\frac{\partial H_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq n}.

Matrix ranks are computed over the corresponding rational function field. We write degxi⁡f\deg_{x_{i}}f for the degree in xix_{i} and deg⁡f\deg f for total degree. The components of HH are linearly independent if no nonzero constant linear form annihilates HH. A polynomial map HH is called normalized if H⁡(0)=0H(0)=0. For a map over a polynomial coefficient ring, normalization in specified polynomial variables means that the constant term in those variables is zero in the coefficient ring.

2.1. Polynomial automorphisms

Let RR be a commutative ring with identity. We denote by GAn⁡(R)\GA_{n}(R) the group of polynomial automorphisms of R⁡[x1,…,xn]R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], represented as polynomial maps and composed by substitution. An elementary automorphism has the form

ei​(f)=(x1,…,xi−1,xi+f,xi+1,…,xn),f∈R⁡[x1,…,xi^,…,xn].e_{i}(f)=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1},x_{i}+f,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{n}),\qquad f\in R[x_{1},\ldots,\widehat{x_{i}},\ldots,x_{n}].

The subgroup generated by these maps is EAn⁡(R)\EA_{n}(R). Constant translations are products of elementary automorphisms.

Definition 2.1.

The tame subgroup is

TAn⁡(R)=⟨GLn⁡(R),EAn⁡(R)⟩⊆GAn⁡(R).\TA_{n}(R)=\langle\GL_{n}(R),\EA_{n}(R)\rangle\subseteq\GA_{n}(R).

An automorphism F∈GAn⁡(R)F\in\GA_{n}(R) is tame over RR if F∈TAn⁡(R)F\in\TA_{n}(R). It is stably tame over RR if, for some m≥0m\geq 0,

F[m]=(F1,…,Fn,xn+1,…,xn+m)∈TAn+m⁡(R).F^{[m]}=(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n},x_{n+1},\ldots,x_{n+m})\in\TA_{n+m}(R).

Equivalently, the tame group is generated by affine and elementary automorphisms. In particular, a triangular automorphism with unit diagonal coefficients is tame. When RR is itself a polynomial ring, tameness over RR treats the variables of the coefficient ring as coefficients. We use this distinction in Section 5.

2.2. Nilpotence and linear conjugation

For a 3×33\times 3 matrix NN over a characteristic-zero domain, let σ2​(N)\sigma_{2}(N) denote the sum of its principal minors of order two. The characteristic polynomial yields

(2.1) N is nilpotent⟺trN=σ2(N)=detN=0.N\text{ is nilpotent}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\tr N=\sigma_{2}(N)=\det N=0.

In this case N3=0N^{3}=0. The stronger identity N2=0N^{2}=0 is not assumed. If J​HJH is nilpotent, then det(I+s​J​H)=1\det(I+sJH)=1 for an indeterminate ss.

For T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\GL_{n}(K), set HT=T∘H∘T−1H^{T}=T\circ H\circ T^{-1}. Then

(2.2) J​HT​(x)=T⁡(J​H)​(T−1​x)​T−1.JH^{T}(x)=T(JH)(T^{-1}x)T^{-1}.

Thus nilpotence, rank, normalization at the origin, and linear independence of the components are preserved. Formula (2.2) requires a constant matrix. Nonlinear coordinates below are used either as auxiliary polynomial coordinates or as explicit factors of id+s​H\id+sH.

We use two known triangularization results. A normalized map whose nilpotent Jacobian has rank at most one has linearly dependent components; see [2] or [8, Theorems 2.3 and 3.4]. A homogeneous map in three variables with nilpotent Jacobian is linearly triangularizable [7]. Consequently, a nonzero homogeneous map G∈K​[x,y,z]3G\in K[x,y,z]^{3} of degree d≥1d\geq 1 with nilpotent Jacobian can be put in the form

(2.3) G=(0,γ​xd,B⁡(x,y)),G=(0,\gamma x^{d},B(x,y)),

where BB is homogeneous of degree dd. For d=1d=1, this is ordinary triangularization of a nilpotent matrix.

2.3. Derivations and slices

Let kk be a field and let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a commutative kk-algebra. A kk-derivation of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a kk-linear map δ:𝒜→𝒜\delta\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A} satisfying the Leibniz rule

δ⁡(f​g)=δ⁡(f)​g+f​δ​(g)(f,g∈𝒜).\delta(fg)=\delta(f)g+f\delta(g)\qquad(f,g\in\mathcal{A}).

Its ring of constants is ker⁡δ={f∈𝒜:δ⁡(f)=0}\ker\delta=\{f\in\mathcal{A}:\delta(f)=0\}; this is a field when 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a field. An element s∈𝒜s\in\mathcal{A} is a slice for δ\delta if δ⁡(s)=1\delta(s)=1. A derivation admitting such an element is called a derivation with a slice. For example, ∂x\partial_{x} on k⁡[x,y,z]k[x,y,z] or k⁡(x,y,z)k(x,y,z) has the slice xx. A derivation δ\delta is locally nilpotent if, for every f∈𝒜f\in\mathcal{A}, there is an integer j≥1j\geq 1 such that δj​(f)=0\delta^{j}(f)=0. Having a slice does not by itself imply local nilpotence.

2.4. Closed polynomials and relative constants

Let kk be any field.

Definition 2.2.

A nonconstant polynomial r∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]r\in k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] is closed if k⁡(r)k(r) is relatively algebraically closed in k⁡(x1,…,xn)k(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}).

In characteristic zero, this is equivalent to k⁡[r]k[r] being integrally closed in the ambient polynomial ring [1, Lemma 3]. We use the closed-generator theorem: a finite family of polynomials generating a field of transcendence degree one is contained in k⁡[r]k[r] for a closed polynomial rr; see [1]. Indeed, choose a generative polynomial for one nonconstant member. Every other member belongs to k⁡(r)k(r) by relative algebraic closedness, and

(2.4) k⁡(r)∩k⁡[x1,…,xn]=k⁡[r].k(r)\cap k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]=k[r].

For completeness, write a rational function as A⁡(r)/B⁡(r)A(r)/B(r) with coprime A,B∈k⁡[t]A,B\in k[t]. A Bézout identity for these polynomials remains valid after substitution. If the quotient is polynomial, B⁡(r)B(r) divides A⁡(r)A(r) in the ambient polynomial ring, so B⁡(r)B(r) is a unit. Hence BB is constant. This last argument does not require closedness.

The following lemma collects the field-theoretic facts used below and specifies the constant field in the generic-fiber argument.

Lemma 2.3.

The following statements hold in characteristic zero.

  1. (i)

    If 𝒦/E\mathcal{K}/E is finitely generated and LL is the relative algebraic closure of EE in 𝒦\mathcal{K}, then L/EL/E is finite and 𝒦/L\mathcal{K}/L is regular. Every finitely generated LL-subalgebra of 𝒦\mathcal{K} is geometrically integral.

  2. (ii)

    A derivation of a field extends uniquely to a finite separable extension. The extensions of commuting derivations commute.

  3. (iii)

    Suppose 𝒦/k⁡(t1,…,tm)\mathcal{K}/k(t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}) is finite separable, and extend the coordinate derivations to 𝒦\mathcal{K}. If a¯∈𝒦\bar{a}\in\mathcal{K} is killed by ∂ti\partial_{t_{i}} for i∈Ii\in I, then a¯\bar{a} is algebraic over k(tj:j∉I)k(t_{j}:j\notin I).

Proof.

For (i), choose a transcendence basis t1,…,trt_{1},\ldots,t_{r} of 𝒦/E\mathcal{K}/E and put d=[𝒦:E(t1,…,tr)]d=[\mathcal{K}:E(t_{1},\ldots,t_{r})]. Every finite intermediate extension L0/EL_{0}/E contained in LL satisfies

[L0:E]=[L0(t1,…,tr):E(t1,…,tr)]≤d.[L_{0}:E]=[L_{0}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{r}):E(t_{1},\ldots,t_{r})]\leq d.

A finite subextension of maximal degree therefore contains every element of LL, which proves finiteness. If an irreducible polynomial over LL factors into monic factors over 𝒦\mathcal{K}, the coefficients of those factors lie in 𝒦\mathcal{K} and are algebraic over LL. They therefore belong to LL, contradicting irreducibility. Since finite extensions in characteristic zero are separable and simple, 𝒦\mathcal{K} is linearly disjoint from every finite extension of LL. Hence 𝒦⊗LL¯\mathcal{K}\otimes_{L}\overline{L} is a domain. Tensoring an inclusion of an LL-subalgebra into 𝒦\mathcal{K} preserves injectivity and proves geometric integrality.

For (ii), if a¯\bar{a} has minimal polynomial P⁡(T)=∑jcj​TjP(T)=\sum_{j}c_{j}T^{j}, an extension of δ\delta must satisfy

δ​a¯=−∑j(δ​cj)​a¯jP′​(a¯).\delta\bar{a}=-\frac{\sum_{j}(\delta c_{j})\bar{a}^{j}}{P^{\prime}(\bar{a})}.

Separability makes the denominator nonzero and gives existence and uniqueness. The commutator of two extended derivations is a derivation that vanishes on the base field and is therefore zero.

For (iii), differentiate the monic minimal polynomial of a¯\bar{a} over k⁡(t1,…,tm)k(t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}). If ∂tia¯=0\partial_{t_{i}}\bar{a}=0, the differentiated polynomial has smaller degree and still annihilates a¯\bar{a}, so it must be zero. Thus its coefficients are killed by every indicated coordinate derivation. Their common constants in the rational function field are k(tj:j∉I)k(t_{j}:j\notin I), which proves the assertion. ∎

The base field is relatively algebraically closed in a purely transcendental extension. In particular, the common constants of all extended coordinate derivations on a subfield of k⁡(x,y,z)k(x,y,z) are kk whenever the preceding lemma applies.

3. A dependent pair of components

The first step is to find two independent constant linear combinations of the components that are algebraically dependent. The following theorem, proved in the remainder of this section, establishes this reduction.

Theorem 3.1 (Dependent pair).

Let H∈K​[x,y,z]3H\in K[x,y,z]^{3} satisfy H⁡(0)=0H(0)=0. Suppose that J​HJH is nilpotent and that the components of HH are linearly independent over KK. Then there exist linearly independent forms ℓ1,ℓ2∈(K3)∗\ell_{1},\ell_{2}\in(K^{3})^{*} such that ℓ1​(H)\ell_{1}(H) and ℓ2​(H)\ell_{2}(H) are algebraically dependent over KK.

We first work over an algebraically closed field kk. Since detJ​H=0\det JH=0, the Jacobian rank is at most two. The dependence result recalled in Section 2 excludes rank at most one. Hence rank⁡J​H=2\rank JH=2. After a simultaneous permutation of source and target coordinates, write H=(u,v,w)H=(u,v,w) with u,vu,v algebraically independent. Set

𝒦=k⁡(x,y,z),E=k⁡(u,v,w),\mathcal{K}=k(x,y,z),\qquad E=k(u,v,w),

and let LL be the relative algebraic closure of EE in 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Then L/k⁡(u,v)L/k(u,v) is finite separable. The derivations ∂u,∂v\partial_{u},\partial_{v} extend uniquely to LL and commute. Put

(3.1) p=wu,q=wv,a=wu​u,b=wu​v,c=wv​v.p=w_{u},\quad q=w_{v},\qquad a=w_{uu},\quad b=w_{uv},\quad c=w_{vv}.

3.1. The embedded generic curve

Consider the Jacobian derivation

D⁡(f)=detJ⁡(u,v,f),(C1,C2,C3)=∇u×∇v.D(f)=\det J(u,v,f),\qquad(C_{1},C_{2},C_{3})=\nabla u\times\nabla v.

By the differential criterion for algebraic dependence,

(3.2) ker𝒦⁡D=L.\ker_{\mathcal{K}}D=L.

Indeed, D⁡(f)=0D(f)=0 is equivalent to ff being algebraic over k⁡(u,v)k(u,v), and E/k⁡(u,v)E/k(u,v) is algebraic.

Since d​w=p​d​u+q​d​v\mathrm{d}w=p\,\mathrm{d}u+q\,\mathrm{d}v, the principal-minor identity is

(3.3) σ2​(J​H)=C3−p​C1−q​C2.\sigma_{2}(JH)=C_{3}-pC_{1}-qC_{2}.

The right-hand side is D⁡(z−p​x−q​y)D(z-px-qy), because p,q∈Lp,q\in L. Thus

(3.4) s=z−p​x−q​y∈L.s=z-px-qy\in L.

Differentiating this identity, and setting

A=a​x+b​y+su,B=b​x+c​y+sv,A=ax+by+s_{u},\qquad B=bx+cy+s_{v},

we obtain

(3.5) A​ux+B​vx=−p,A​uy+B​vy=−q,A​uz+B​vz=1.Au_{x}+Bv_{x}=-p,\qquad Au_{y}+Bv_{y}=-q,\qquad Au_{z}+Bv_{z}=1.

These equations imply

tr⁡J​H=ux+vy+p​uz+q​vz=−A​C1−B​C2.\tr JH=u_{x}+v_{y}+pu_{z}+qv_{z}=-AC_{1}-BC_{2}.

The coefficients of A,BA,B, viewed as affine expressions in x,yx,y, lie in LL. It follows that

(3.6) τ=12​a​x2+b​x​y+12​c​y2+su​x+sv​y∈L.\tau=\tfrac{1}{2}ax^{2}+bxy+\tfrac{1}{2}cy^{2}+s_{u}x+s_{v}y\in L.
Proposition 3.2.

Let 𝒞=Spec⁡L⁡[x,y,z]\mathcal{C}=\Spec L[x,y,z], where L⁡[x,y,z]L[x,y,z] denotes the subalgebra of 𝒦\mathcal{K} generated by the source coordinates. Then 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a geometrically integral embedded affine line or plane conic. In the conic case its points at infinity have directions

(3.7) e=(ξ,η,p​ξ+q​η),a​ξ2+2​b​ξ​η+c​η2=0,e=(\xi,\eta,p\xi+q\eta),\qquad a\xi^{2}+2b\xi\eta+c\eta^{2}=0,

over L¯\overline{L}.

Proof.

This algebra has fraction field 𝒦\mathcal{K} and dimension one over LL. It is geometrically integral by Lemma 2.3. Equations (3.4) and (3.6) place the curve in the plane Z=p​X+q​Y+sZ=pX+qY+s and on the quadratic

Φ⁡(X,Y)=12​a​X2+b​X​Y+12​c​Y2+su​X+sv​Y−τ.\Phi(X,Y)=\tfrac{1}{2}aX^{2}+bXY+\tfrac{1}{2}cY^{2}+s_{u}X+s_{v}Y-\tau.

The coefficients a,b,ca,b,c are not all zero. Otherwise, both coordinate derivations on LL annihilate p,qp,q, so they belong to kk. The same argument gives w−p​u−q​v∈kw-pu-qv\in k. Evaluating at the origin then contradicts linear independence.

The kernel of L⁡[X,Y]→𝒦L[X,Y]\to\mathcal{K}, X↦xX\mapsto x, Y↦yY\mapsto y, is a height-one prime containing the nonzero polynomial Φ\Phi. It is generated by an irreducible factor of Φ\Phi, of degree one or two. If the degree is two, that factor is a scalar multiple of Φ\Phi. Homogenizing the plane and quadratic equations gives (3.7). ∎

The direction space of the containing affine plane is

(3.8) 𝒯={(ξ,η,pξ+qη):ξ,η∈L}.\mathcal{T}=\{(\xi,\eta,p\xi+q\eta):\xi,\eta\in L\}.

After extending scalars to 𝒦\mathcal{K}, this is the column space of J​HJH. No nonzero constant linear form vanishes on 𝒯\mathcal{T}, since such a form would satisfy ℓ​J​H=0\ell JH=0, and hence ℓ⁡(H)=0\ell(H)=0 by normalization.

The construction is compatible with constant conjugation. For S∈GL3⁡(k)S\in\GL_{3}(k), regard x′=S​xx^{\prime}=Sx and H′=S​HH^{\prime}=SH as elements of the same field 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Then k⁡(H′)=Ek(H^{\prime})=E, L⁡[x′]=L⁡[x]L[x^{\prime}]=L[x], and the Jacobian in the new coordinates is S⁡(J​H)​S−1S(JH)S^{-1}. The transformation SS acts on the embedded curve, its directions, and 𝒯\mathcal{T}. We may therefore repeat the construction with any algebraically independent pair of the new components.

3.2. Constant planes at infinity

Let Hd≠0H_{d}\neq 0 be the highest homogeneous part of HH. Taking the highest homogeneous part of the identity (J​H)3=0(JH)^{3}=0 gives (J​Hd)3=0(JH_{d})^{3}=0. The polynomial Hi​(X,Y,Z)−Hi​(x,y,z)H_{i}(X,Y,Z)-H_{i}(x,y,z), with coefficients in LL, vanishes on 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Therefore every direction at infinity lies in one of the constant planes in (3.9).

3.3. Excluding a line

Suppose that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a line. Choose a constant form mm that vanishes on its direction and use mm as the first row of a simultaneous change of coordinates. The new coordinate xx is constant on the geometric line, so it is algebraic over LL. Relative algebraic closedness gives x∈Lx\in L.

3.4. Excluding two points at infinity

Suppose that the conic has two distinct directions e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} over L¯\overline{L}. Choose constant forms m1,m2m_{1},m_{2} with mi​(ei)=0m_{i}(e_{i})=0. Lemma 3.3.

A polynomial map (u,v,γ​u​v+α​u+β​v+δ)(u,v,\gamma uv+\alpha u+\beta v+\delta) with γ≠0\gamma\neq 0 cannot have both a nilpotent Jacobian and Jacobian rank two.

If degz⁡v≥2\deg_{z}v\geq 2, the term v​vzvv_{z} in (3.13) has strictly larger zz-degree than the other terms. Therefore v=C​z+Dv=Cz+D with C≠0C\neq 0. The coefficient of zz gives Cx+γ​C2=0C_{x}+\gamma C^{2}=0, which is impossible by comparing degrees in xx. ∎

The conic therefore has a unique point at infinity, counted twice. Let ee be its direction and choose a nonzero constant form mm with m⁡(e)=0m(e)=0. Use mm as the first row of a simultaneous coordinate change. The first component u=m⁡(H)u=m(H) is nonconstant. Choose a constant combination vv algebraically independent of uu, complete the coordinate change, and repeat the construction of the curve.

Now ex=0e_{x}=0, and (3.8) implies ey≠0e_{y}\neq 0. The double root of the binary quadratic in (3.7) is [0:1][0:1]. Hence a≠0a\neq 0 and b=c=0b=c=0. Both coordinate derivatives of wvw_{v} vanish, so wv=μ∈kw_{v}=\mu\in k. It follows that

d⁡(w−μ​v)=wu​d​u.\mathrm{d}(w-\mu v)=w_{u}\,\mathrm{d}u.

We give the field-theoretic justification for the resulting algebraic dependence. The extension L/k⁡(u,v)L/k(u,v) is finite separable, and the extended coordinate derivation ∂v\partial_{v} satisfies

∂v(w−μ​v)=wv−μ=0.\partial_{v}(w-\mu v)=w_{v}-\mu=0.

By Lemma 2.3(iii), w−μ​vw-\mu v is therefore algebraic over k⁡(u)k(u). More explicitly, let P​(T)∈k​(u,v)​[T]P(T)\in k(u,v)[T] be its monic minimal polynomial. The coefficients of PP thus belong to the constant field of ∂v\partial_{v} on k⁡(u,v)k(u,v), which is k⁡(u)k(u). The corresponding constant forms are independent. This proves Theorem 3.1 over an algebraically closed field.

3.6. Descent and completion of the proof

We use Proposition 4.2, which is proved in the next section over an arbitrary characteristic-zero field, assuming that a dependent pair is already defined over that field. Its proof does not use Theorem 3.1.

Extend scalars from KK to K¯\overline{K}. Linear independence of the components is preserved, since it is a rank condition on their coefficient matrix. The preceding argument and Proposition 4.2 give the canonical form over K¯\overline{K}. Consider the finite-dimensional relation space

(3.14) VK={R∈K​[U,V,W]≤2:R⁡(H1,H2,H3)=0}.V_{K}=\{R\in K[U,V,W]_{\leq 2}:R(H_{1},H_{2},H_{3})=0\}.

VK⊗KK¯=VK¯.V_{K}\otimes_{K}\overline{K}=V_{\overline{K}}.

For 𝒩P\mathcal{N}_{P}, the first two components are algebraically independent and the third is the square of the first. Its full ideal of relations is (W−U2)(W-U^{2}), whose subspace of relations of degree at most two is one-dimensional. Constant linear target changes preserve total degree, and source changes preserve relations. Consequently dimKVK=1\dim_{K}V_{K}=1.

Choose 0≠R∈VK0\neq R\in V_{K}. Its constant term is zero because H⁡(0)=0H(0)=0. Over K¯\overline{K}, its quadratic part has rank one. The rank is also one over KK, so

R=κℓ2+ℓ′,κ∈K∗,ℓ,ℓ′∈(K3)∗.R=\kappa\ell^{2}+\ell^{\prime},\qquad\kappa\in K^{*},\quad\ell,\ell^{\prime}\in(K^{3})^{*}.

Here a symmetric rank-one matrix over KK can be written as a nonzero scalar times an outer square over KK by choosing a nonzero diagonal entry. This does not require a square root. The forms ℓ,ℓ′\ell,\ell^{\prime} are independent. Otherwise ℓ′=c​ℓ\ell^{\prime}=c\ell and

ℓ⁡(H)​(κ​ℓ​(H)+c)=0.\ell(H)\bigl(\kappa\ell(H)+c\bigr)=0.

The polynomial ring is a domain, so ℓ⁡(H)\ell(H) is constant. Its value at the origin is zero, contradicting independence of the components. Finally,

ℓ′​(H)=−κ​ℓ​(H)2\ell^{\prime}(H)=-\kappa\ell(H)^{2}

is the required algebraic dependence over KK. This completes the proof of Theorem 3.1.∎

4. Classification and tameness

We now pass from the dependent pair in Theorem 3.1 to a canonical form. The classification rests on a polynomial calculation over the original field.

Theorem 4.1 (Classification).

Let H∈K​[x,y,z]3H\in K[x,y,z]^{3} satisfy H⁡(0)=0H(0)=0, and suppose that its components are linearly independent over KK. Then J​HJH is nilpotent if and only if there exist T∈GL3⁡(K)T\in\GL_{3}(K) and a nonconstant polynomial P∈K⁡[t]P\in K[t], with P⁡(0)=0P(0)=0, such that

(4.1) T∘H∘T−1=𝒩P,𝒩P=(P⁡(y+x2),z−2​x​P​(y+x2),P​(y+x2)2).T\circ H\circ T^{-1}=\mathcal{N}_{P},\qquad\mathcal{N}_{P}=\bigl(P(y+x^{2}),\ z-2xP(y+x^{2}),\ P(y+x^{2})^{2}\bigr).

The theorem describes a family of normal forms; it does not assert that PP is unique under linear conjugation. We prove the algebraic part separately for use in the descent in Section 3.

Proposition 4.2.

Let H∈K​[x,y,z]3H\in K[x,y,z]^{3} be normalized, with nilpotent Jacobian and linearly independent components. The forward implication follows from Theorem 3.1 and Proposition 4.2. For the converse, put ρ=y+x2\rho=y+x^{2}, u=P⁡(ρ)u=P(\rho), and q¯=P′​(ρ)\bar{q}=P^{\prime}(\rho). Then

Remark 4.3.

Theorem 4.1 provides an affirmative answer to Problem 3.8 in [21] and Problem 4.1 in [13].

4.4. The generic curve of the canonical family

The canonical family gives an explicit model for the relative constant field used in Section 3. Put

ρ=y+x2,u=P⁡(ρ),v=z−2​x​u.\rho=y+x^{2},\qquad u=P(\rho),\qquad v=z-2xu.

Since the third component of 𝒩P\mathcal{N}_{P} is u2u^{2}, the image field and its relative algebraic closure in 𝒦=K⁡(x,y,z)\mathcal{K}=K(x,y,z) are

(4.24) E=K(u,v),L=K(ρ,v),𝒦=L(x),[L:E]=degP.E=K(u,v),\qquad L=K(\rho,v),\qquad\mathcal{K}=L(x),\qquad[L:E]=\deg P.

Indeed, y=ρ−x2y=\rho-x^{2} and z=v+2​x​P​(ρ)z=v+2xP(\rho), so 𝒦=L⁡(x)\mathcal{K}=L(x). The field LL is relatively algebraically closed in this purely transcendental extension. Moreover, L/EL/E is finite of degree deg⁡P\deg P, the degree of the univariate extension K⁡(ρ)/K⁡(P⁡(ρ))K(\rho)/K(P(\rho)) after adjoining the independent variable vv.

Over LL, the embedded generic curve has the parametrization

(4.25) x⟼(x,ρ−x2,v+2​P​(ρ)​x).x\longmapsto\bigl(x,\ \rho-x^{2},\ v+2P(\rho)x\bigr).

It is a parabola in the containing affine plane, with the unique direction at infinity [0:1:0][0:1:0]. If deg⁡P>1\deg P>1, the geometric generic fiber over EE has several components, corresponding to the distinct generic roots of P⁡(ρ)=uP(\rho)=u. Passing to LL selects one geometrically integral component. This explains the use of the relative algebraic closure in the proof of Proposition 3.2.

The source coordinate ρ\rho and the target relation W−U2=0W-U^{2}=0 have different roles. The source coordinate describes the conic fibers, whereas the target relation defines the one-dimensional relation space used in the descent in Section 3.

We now consider higher-dimensional extensions, separating the base variables from the last three variables. Let n≥6n\geq 6, put m=n−6m=n-6, and write

where A∈K​[ι]3A\in K[\iota]^{3}, C∈K​[ι]mC\in K[\iota]^{m}, and B∈R​[ψ]3B\in R[\psi]^{3}.

For a field KK, we use the notation

OPEN−ϑ1​h​(ϑ1​r1+ϑ2​r2)+d2, 0),\displaystyle-\vartheta_{1}h(\vartheta_{1}r_{1}+\vartheta_{2}r_{2})+d_{2},\ 0\bigr),

where ϑ1,ϑ2,d1,d2∈K⁡[r3]\vartheta_{1},\vartheta_{2},d_{1},d_{2}\in K[r_{3}], (ϑ1,ϑ2)=K⁡[r3](\vartheta_{1},\vartheta_{2})=K[r_{3}], and h∈K​[r3]​[t]h\in K[r_{3}][t] with h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0. We retain 𝒩P\mathcal{N}_{P} for the independent family (4.1).

5.1. Normal forms of the two blocks

Theorem 5.1 (Blockwise normal forms).

Suppose that H~\widetilde{H} has the form (5.1), H~​(0)=0\widetilde{H}(0)=0, and J​H~J\widetilde{H} is nilpotent. Then the following statements hold.

Remark 5.2.

The theorem concerns the two three-variable diagonal blocks. A matrix with entries in K⁡(ζ)K(\zeta) is constant for differentiation in ψ\psi, but need not be constant for the full Jacobian. Thus (5.3) cannot be substituted into (2.2) for the full map. In particular, the notation T∘H~∘T−1T\circ\widetilde{H}\circ T^{-1} with T∈GLn⁡(K⁡(ζ))T\in\GL_{n}(K(\zeta)) does not by itself define a constant linear conjugation of H~\widetilde{H}. Formula (5.4) also shows why the middle block changes when the first three source coordinates change.

The subtraction of χ⁡(ζ)\chi(\zeta) is necessary even when H~​(0)=0\widetilde{H}(0)=0.

Example 5.3.

Take n=6n=6, A=0A=0, and

B⁡(ζ,ψ)=(ε,ψ3−2​ψ1​ε,ε2+ζ1),ε=ψ2+ψ12.B(\zeta,\psi)=\bigl(\varepsilon,\ \psi_{3}-2\psi_{1}\varepsilon,\ \varepsilon^{2}+\zeta_{1}\bigr),\qquad\varepsilon=\psi_{2}+\psi_{1}^{2}.

The full map (0,0,0,B)(0,0,0,B) vanishes at the origin and has nilpotent Jacobian by (5.5) and (4.16). Over L=K⁡(ζ1,ζ2,ζ3)L=K(\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2},\zeta_{3}), its last three components are linearly independent. Their relation ideal is

because ε\varepsilon and ψ3−2​ψ1​ε\psi_{3}-2\psi_{1}\varepsilon are algebraically independent. In particular, every nonzero relation of total degree at most two has a nonzero constant term.

A dependent form (5.2) has a nonzero linear relation. A canonical form 𝒩Q\mathcal{N}_{Q} has the quadratic relation W−U2=0W-U^{2}=0, whose constant term is zero, even if one allows Q⁡(0)≠0Q(0)\neq 0. Constant linear target changes preserve the constant term of a relation, and source changes preserve the relation ideal. Therefore BB is not linearly conjugate over LL to either displayed family. After subtracting B⁡(ζ,0)=(0,0,ζ1)B(\zeta,0)=(0,0,\zeta_{1}), the resulting map is exactly 𝒩t\mathcal{N}_{t}.

5.2. Automorphisms over the base ring

The normal form over the fraction field alone does not establish stable tameness over RR. We first prove polynomial invertibility over RR.

Lemma 5.4.

Let RR be a domain, L=Frac⁡RL=\Frac R, and let G∈R​[ψ1,…,ψr]rG\in R[\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{r}]^{r} satisfy G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0 and J​G​(0)∈GLr⁡(R)JG(0)\in\GL_{r}(R). If G∈GAr⁡(L)G\in\GA_{r}(L), then G∈GAr⁡(R)G\in\GA_{r}(R).

Proof.

The formal inverse theorem over a ring gives a unique inverse Q∈R​[[ψ]]rQ\in R[[\psi]]^{r} with Q⁡(0)=0Q(0)=0. It can be constructed degree by degree: after the terms below degree dd are known, the degree-dd correction is obtained by multiplying the degree-dd error by J​G​(0)−1JG(0)^{-1}. Thus all coefficients lie in RR.

The polynomial inverse of GG over LL fixes the origin. As an element of L​[[ψ]]rL[[\psi]]^{r}, it equals QQ by uniqueness. Hence QQ has only finitely many nonzero coefficients and belongs to R​[ψ]rR[\psi]^{r}. Both inverse identities hold over RR, either by the formal construction or by the injection R⁡[ψ]↪L⁡[ψ]R[\psi]\hookrightarrow L[\psi]. ∎

Proposition 5.5.

Let R=K⁡[ζ1,…,ζr]R=K[\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{r}], and let B∈R​[ψ1,ψ2,ψ3]3B\in R[\psi_{1},\psi_{2},\psi_{3}]^{3} have nilpotent Jacobian Jψ​BJ_{\psi}B. Then

Θ⁡(ψ)=ψ+B⁡(ζ,ψ)\Theta(\psi)=\psi+B(\zeta,\psi)

is a polynomial automorphism over RR and is stably tame over RR.

Proof.

Put χ=B⁡(ζ,0)\chi=B(\zeta,0) and G⁡(ψ)=ψ+B⁡(ζ,ψ)−χG(\psi)=\psi+B(\zeta,\psi)-\chi. Then G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0. The matrix N=Jψ​B​(ζ,0)N=J_{\psi}B(\zeta,0) satisfies N3=0N^{3}=0, so

J​G​(0)=I+N∈GL3⁡(R),(I+N)−1=I−N+N2.JG(0)=I+N\in\GL_{3}(R),\qquad(I+N)^{-1}=I-N+N^{2}.

Over L=Frac⁡RL=\Frac R, Theorem 4.6 implies that GG is a polynomial automorphism. Lemma 5.4 gives G∈GA3⁡(R)G\in\GA_{3}(R). Since Θ=Transχ∘G\Theta=\operatorname{Trans}_{\chi}\circ G, we also have Θ∈GA3⁡(R)\Theta\in\GA_{3}(R).

For every prime 𝔭∈Spec⁡R\mathfrak{p}\in\Spec R, let κ⁡(𝔭)\kappa(\mathfrak{p}) be the residue field. It contains KK, so it has characteristic zero. Nilpotence is expressed by a polynomial matrix identity and is therefore preserved under specialization. Thus

Θ𝔭=ψ+B𝔭​(ψ)∈TA3⁡(κ⁡(𝔭))\Theta_{\mathfrak{p}}=\psi+B_{\mathfrak{p}}(\psi)\in\TA_{3}(\kappa(\mathfrak{p}))

by Theorem 4.6. The ring RR is regular. The residue-field criterion [3, Theorem 4.12] therefore implies that Θ\Theta is stably tame over RR. ∎

5.3. Stable tameness of the full map

Theorem 5.6 (Stable tameness of block extensions).

Let n≥6n\geq 6 and let H~∈K​[x1,…,xn]n\widetilde{H}\in K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]^{n} have nilpotent Jacobian J​H~J\widetilde{H} and satisfy

Hi∈K⁡[x1,x2,x3](1≤i≤n−3).H_{i}\in K[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}]\qquad(1\leq i\leq n-3).

Then F=id+H~F=\id+\widetilde{H} is a polynomial automorphism and is stably tame over KK. In particular, this holds for the maps of Theorem 5.1.

Proof.

Write FF in block form:

(5.6) F⁡(ζ,ψ)\displaystyle F(\zeta,\psi) =(F0​(ζ),Θζ​(ψ)),\displaystyle=\bigl(F_{0}(\zeta),\Theta_{\zeta}(\psi)\bigr),
F0​(ι,φ)\displaystyle F_{0}(\iota,\varphi) =(ι+A(ι),φ+C(ι)),Θζ(ψ)=ψ+B(ζ,ψ).\displaystyle=(\iota+A(\iota),\varphi+C(\iota)),\qquad\Theta_{\zeta}(\psi)=\psi+B(\zeta,\psi).

The diagonal blocks in (5.5) are nilpotent. By Theorem 4.6, g⁡(ι)=ι+A⁡(ι)g(\iota)=\iota+A(\iota) is tame over KK. The base automorphism factors as

F0=(ι,φ+C⁡(g−1​(ι)))∘(g⁡(ι),φ).F_{0}=(\iota,\varphi+C(g^{-1}(\iota)))\circ(g(\iota),\varphi).

The first factor is a product of elementary maps, one for each middle coordinate. Hence F0F_{0} is tame. For m=0m=0, this factor is the identity.

By Proposition 5.5, Θ∈GA3⁡(R)\Theta\in\GA_{3}(R) is stably tame over R=K⁡[ζ]R=K[\zeta]. Thus (Θ,ψ4,…,ψ3+s)∈TA3+s⁡(R)(\Theta,\psi_{4},\ldots,\psi_{3+s})\in\TA_{3+s}(R) for some s≥0s\geq 0. An elementary factor over RR is elementary over KK after the base variables ζ\zeta are included and held fixed. To treat the linear factors, use Suslin’s theorem in the form

(5.7) GLl⁡(K⁡[ζ])=⟨El​(K⁡[ζ]),GLl⁡(K)⟩,l≥3;\GL_{l}(K[\zeta])=\langle E_{l}(K[\zeta]),\GL_{l}(K)\rangle,\qquad l\geq 3;

see [3, Theorem 3.23]. Each elementary matrix in (5.7) lifts to an elementary polynomial automorphism over KK, while a matrix in GLl⁡(K)\GL_{l}(K) is linear over KK. It follows that Ψ⁡(ζ,ψ)=(ζ,Θζ​(ψ))\Psi(\zeta,\psi)=(\zeta,\Theta_{\zeta}(\psi)) is stably tame over KK.

Finally, F=(F0​(ζ),ψ)∘ΨF=(F_{0}(\zeta),\psi)\circ\Psi. The first factor is tame and the second is stably tame. Their composition is tame after a common stabilization. This also establishes polynomial invertibility. Explicitly, for a target (ϖ,z)(\varpi,z) one first sets ζ=F0−1​(ϖ)\zeta=F_{0}^{-1}(\varpi) and then ψ=Θζ−1​(z)\psi=\Theta_{\zeta}^{-1}(z); the coefficients of Θ−1\Theta^{-1} lie in RR by Proposition 5.5. ∎

Remark 5.7.

Normalization of H~\widetilde{H} is not needed in Theorem 5.6, because Theorem 4.6 allows arbitrary constant terms and Proposition 5.5 explicitly subtracts the relative constant term. The argument gives no uniform bound on the number of stabilizing variables. It also does not assert tameness of the full map without stabilization.

6. Concluding remarks

The three-dimensional argument consists of a geometric reduction followed by a polynomial calculation. The generic-fiber construction uses the trace and principal-minor identities to obtain a plane equation and a quadratic equation. Homogeneous triangularization then restricts the directions at infinity. Once a dependent pair is available, the normal form and its tame factorization follow from the derivation argument of Proposition 4.2. The descent uses the one-dimensional space of quadratic relations, so the final conjugating maps are defined over the original field.

The canonical family also gives several explicit consequences. If d=deg⁡P≥1d=\deg P\geq 1, then

deg⁡𝒩P=4​d,rank⁡J​𝒩P=2.\deg\mathcal{N}_{P}=4d,\qquad\rank J\mathcal{N}_{P}=2.

The minor in rows 1,21,2 and columns 2,32,3 of (4.16) is P′​(y+x2)≠0P^{\prime}(y+x^{2})\neq 0. The (1,3)(1,3) entry of (J​𝒩P)2(J\mathcal{N}_{P})^{2} is the same nonzero polynomial. Thus the nilpotency index is exactly three. The classification therefore implies that every normalized map in dimension three with nilpotent Jacobian and linearly independent components has degree divisible by four. This is a consequence of the proposed general theorem, whereas the displayed degree, rank, and nilpotency-index calculations for the canonical family are direct.

For the block extensions, the distinction between coefficients and polynomial variables is essential. The last three components must first be normalized over the fraction field of the base ring. The resulting linear normal form need not arise from a change of coordinates over the polynomial ring. Stable tameness follows from a separate argument: polynomial inversion descends through the formal inverse at the origin, and residue-field tameness permits the application of the regular-ring criterion. This argument does not require descent of the rational conjugating matrices.

The recent work of Castañeda, Honorato, and Valenzuela-Henríquez [4, Theorems 1.2, 5.1, and 8.1] connects Keller maps with the weak Markus–Yamabe injectivity problem. Starting from a real Keller map F=id+HF=\id+H with H⁡(0)=J​H​(0)=0H(0)=JH(0)=0 and component degrees did_{i}, their chain realization constructs a polynomial vector field XF,βX_{F,\beta} satisfying

N=∑i=1nmax{di,2}−n,Spec(JXF,β(Z))={−1}(Z∈ℝN).N=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\max\{d_{i},2\}-n,\qquad\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(JX_{F,\beta}(Z)\bigr)=\{-1\}\quad(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{N}).

Its equilibria correspond polynomially to F−1​(β)F^{-1}(\beta). Component degrees (4,6,7)(4,6,7) yield a degree-seven vector field in dimension 1414 with three rational equilibria. A separate construction yields a degree-three vector field in dimension 1818. Adjoining negative identity vector fields extends the counterexamples to every dimension at least 1414.

For these fields, R=id+XR=\id+X has nilpotent Jacobian, whereas id−R=−X\id-R=-X is noninjective. Thus nilpotence alone does not imply invertibility in arbitrary dimension. The constructions do not impose the variable dependence required by the block theorems of Section 5.

In dimension three, Theorem 4.6 gives injectivity for the constant-spectrum class X=−id+HX=-\id+H with J​HJH nilpotent. This does not settle the general Hurwitz case, where the eigenvalues need only have negative real parts. The cited work leaves dimensions 33 through 1313 unresolved.

Several questions lie beyond the scope of these arguments. In dimension four, can the nilpotence identities control the degree of the embedded generic curve when the Jacobian rank is three? Under which additional hypotheses can two independent constant linear combinations of the components be made algebraically dependent? For the block extensions, can one bound the required stabilization in terms of the dimension or degrees? Answering these questions requires additional arguments; the three-dimensional plane-conic calculation does not extend formally to a general higher-dimensional map.
